coinage.standard: aureus 1/40 lb (c. 7.9-8.0 g) = 25 denarii; denarius 1/84 lb (c. 3.9 g), c. 97-98% silver; sestertius (orichalcum, c. 25-27 g) = 4 asses; dupondius (orichalcum) = 2 asses; as (copper) = 1/16 denarius
coinage.text: Augustus turned the improvised coinages of the civil wars into a system that lasted 250 years. Gold became a regular denomination, fixed at 25 denarii. From c. 23 BC the moneyers at Rome again struck base metal, now in two alloys whose colour marked value: yellow orichalcum (brass, a zinc-copper alloy produced by cementation) for the sestertius and dupondius, red copper for the as and quadrans. The quadrans was the price of a bath. The moneyers' names (IIIVIR AAAFF) appear around a large SC until c. 4 BC, after which aes carries the emperor's portrait. Gold and silver moved to Lugdunum c. 15 BC. In the provinces, Augustus allowed cities and colonies to keep their own bronze and the East its silver (cistophori, Alexandrian tetradrachms, Antiochene tetradrachms), producing the dual system of 'imperial' and 'provincial' coinage that collectors still use. Values for prices: a legionary was paid 225 denarii a year (900 sesterces) until Domitian.
scholarship: RIC I² (Sutherland 1984)
Burnett, Amandry and Ripollès, Roman Provincial Coinage I (1992)
Wolters, Nummi signati (1999)

coinage.t: What does SC on imperial bronze mean?
coinage.text: From the Augustan reform to the 260s almost all Rome-mint bronze bears SC (senatus consulto), while gold and silver do not. The old view (Mommsen) was that the Senate controlled bronze and the emperor precious metals. Most numismatists now reject a division of minting authority: the formula refers to a senatorial decree authorising the issue, honouring the emperor, or legitimising the token value of the base-metal coinage, and the emperor controlled the whole mint. SC also appears on Antioch's bronze, struck for the governor of Syria. Its disappearance in the 260s, with the end of the sestertius, marks the death of the Augustan system.
scholarship: Kraft, 'S(enatus) C(onsulto)', JNG 12 (1962)
Burnett, 'The authority to coin in the late Republic and early Empire', NC 1977
Wolters, Nummi signati (1999)

coinage.text: TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS / PONTIF MAXIM, a seated woman holding sceptre and branch (often identified as Livia as Pax or Iustitia). Struck at Lugdunum in great numbers through Tiberius' reign, it is traditionally identified with the denarius shown to Jesus in the Gospels ('Whose image and inscription is this?', Mark 12.13-17). Whether this particular type or older denarii of Augustus circulated in Judaea in the 30s is uncertain, but the identification has made it one of the most collected ancient coins. Three main variants exist by the chair's legs (plain or ornate) and the presence of a footstool; ornate-leg types are earlier. Many modern fakes and ancient plated copies.
scholarship: RIC I² Tiberius 26-30
Giard, Le monnayage de l'atelier de Lyon (1983)

coinage.text: Small stamps punched into circulating bronze revalidated, recalled or advertised. VAR on asses in Germany belongs to Quinctilius Varus (6-9) and helped identify Kalkriese; IMP AVG and AVG on Altar asses and Nemausus coins; TIB, TIB AVG and TIB IMP on Augustan coins in the Rhine camps; NCAPR (debated: Nero Claudius Augustus Probavit?) on Claudian and Neronian aes in Italy; PROB and BON(um) as approval marks; SPQR, IMP VES and other marks in the civil war of 68-69 (Galba and Vespasian's partisans validating old coins and erasing the names of Caligula, whose coins were defaced after his assassination). Countermarks are a primary source for circulation, military pay and political memory, and specialist studies (Werz, Pangerl) exploit them.
scholarship: Howgego, Greek Imperial Countermarks (1985)
Werz, Gegenstempel auf Aes-Prägungen der frühen römischen Kaiserzeit (2009)

coinage.standard: aureus cut from 1/40 to 1/45 lb (c. 7.3 g); denarius from 1/84 to 1/96 lb (c. 3.4 g) and fineness reduced (Walker c. 93%; Butcher and Ponting c. 80%)
coinage.text: In the year of the Great Fire, Nero reduced the weight of gold and silver and, on recent metallurgical analysis (Butcher and Ponting 2014), cut the fineness of the denarius much more than Walker's surface analyses implied, probably also adding silver from older coins recalled and restruck. Pliny notes the lighter aureus. At the same time the mint, back at Rome after decades at Lugdunum, began a remarkable bronze programme: experimental orichalcum asses and semisses, value marks (II on dupondii, I on asses), and some of the finest portrait sestertii ever struck, with types of the harbour of Ostia (PORT AVG), the Temple of Janus closed (PACE P R TERRA MARIQ PARTA IANVM CLVSIT), the Macellum Magnum and the Congiarium. Why it matters: it is the first deliberate debasement of the imperial silver, a fiscal response to the costs of rebuilding Rome and the Golden House, and it set the denarius on its long path of decline.
scholarship: Butcher and Ponting, The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage (2014)
MacDowall, The Western Coinages of Nero (1979)

coinage.text: Between Vindex's revolt (spring 68) and Vespasian's victory (December 69) Gaul, Spain, Africa and the Rhine produced coins with no emperor's portrait, the so-called 'autonomous' issues: SIGNA P R, GENIO P R, FIDES EXERCITVVM, SALVS GENERIS HVMANI, LIBERTAS RESTITVTA, ROMA RENASC. Some belong to Vindex and his allies in Gaul, some to Galba in Spain, some to the German legions before they proclaimed Vitellius, and one rare group to L. Clodius Macer, legate of Africa, with his bare head and PRO PRAE AFRICAE. They give a unique view of Republican and military slogans in a war between armies. All are rare to very rare, and attribution of individual groups is debated (Martin, Kraay).
scholarship: Martin, Die anonymen Münzen des Jahres 68 nach Christus (1974)
Kraay, 'The coinage of Vindex and Galba', NC 1949
RIC I² Civil Wars

coinage.text: Vespasian and Titus celebrated the suppression of the Jewish revolt and the destruction of the Temple (70) with one of the longest-running victory series in Roman coinage. Typical sestertius: a Jewess seated mourning beneath a palm, with the emperor or a bound Jewish captive standing, IVDAEA CAPTA S C. Denarii read IVDAEA under a mourning figure, with a trophy. Greek-legend versions (IOYΔAIAΣ EAΛΩKYIAΣ) were struck at Caesarea Maritima. The series is iconographically linked with the reliefs of the Arch of Titus. Very popular; sestertii in good condition are expensive and frequently faked or tooled.
scholarship: RIC II.1² (Carradice and Buttrey 2007)
Meshorer, A Treasury of Jewish Coins (2001)

coinage.t: Domitian restores the silver (82) and partially retreats (85)
coinage.standard: 82-85: denarius c. 3.5 g at about 98% silver (Augustan purity); 85 on: c. 3.4 g at about 92%
coinage.text: Early in his reign Domitian raised the fineness of the denarius back to Augustan standards and the weight of the aureus, an extraordinary act among emperors. In 85 or soon after, when he raised legionary pay by a third (from 300 to 400 denarii, or 900 to 1,200 sesterces), he lowered the silver to roughly the post-64 level. His denarii are therefore a test case for the relationship between army pay, bullion supply and coin quality. Domitianic denarii from 82-85 can sometimes be recognised by their brighter silver and are dated by his consulships (COS VIII-XI) and tribunician years. His long Minerva series (four reverse types repeated annually) makes his denarii easy to date by legend.
scholarship: Carradice, Coinage and Finances in the Reign of Domitian (1983)
Butcher and Ponting (2014)

coinage.t: Restored coins: Titus, Domitian, Nerva and Trajan
coinage.text: The Flavians and Nerva re-struck earlier imperial bronze types with an added legend REST (restituit), honouring Augustus, Agrippa, Livia, Drusus, Germanicus, Claudius and Galba: a programme of dynastic memory. Trajan went further around 107, issuing restored denarii and aurei of Republican moneyers' types (from the Dioscuri to Caesar's) and of earlier emperors, each with IMP CAES TRAIAN AVG GER DAC P P REST. This came with Trajan's recall and melting of worn old coin reported by Dio. Restored issues are rare to very rare and attractive to collectors of both Republic and Empire; beware tooling and modern fantasy 'restitutions'.
scholarship: Komnick, Die Restitutionsmünzen der frühen Kaiserzeit (2001)
Woytek, Die Reichsprägung des Kaisers Traianus (2010)

coinage.standard: fineness reduced from c. 90% to c. 80% (Butcher and Ponting)
coinage.text: Cassius Dio says that Trajan 'melted down all the worn coinage'. Hoard evidence shows the disappearance of pre-64 denarii in the decades after, and analyses show a fall in fineness at the same date, implying that Trajan profited from the recoinage after the Dacian wars, despite the vast Dacian booty claimed by later sources (John Lydus, citing Crito, of 5 million pounds of gold, a figure no one believes). The 'restored' issues of c. 107 commemorated the coins being withdrawn. Trajan's own denarius types celebrate Dacia, the Forum and Column, the Via Traiana and the Danube bridge.
scholarship: Woytek, Die Reichsprägung des Kaisers Traianus (2010)
Butcher and Ponting (2014)

coinage.text: During his eastern tour Hadrian ordered a massive recoinage of the silver of Asia Minor at several mints, producing cistophori with cult images of individual cities: Artemis of Ephesus, the temple of Zeus at Pergamum, the Capitoline temple, Diana Lucifera, the image of the city of Nicomedia. Many were overstruck on older cistophori of Antony, Augustus and Claudius, whose undertypes are often visible. It is a key source for Hadrian's dealings with the Greek cities and for provincial cults. Metcalf's die study is the standard work.
scholarship: Metcalf, The Cistophori of Hadrian (1980)

coinage.standard: denarius fineness falling from c. 80% (early Pius) to c. 75% (Marcus) and c. 70% (Commodus) on traditional figures
coinage.text: The fineness of the denarius slipped through the 2nd century and fell more sharply under Marcus Aurelius during the Marcomannic wars and the Antonine plague, when the emperor famously auctioned palace treasures in the Forum of Trajan to pay for the war rather than raise taxes (HA Marcus 17). Commodus cut the weight in 186-187. The silver supply from Spain declined in the same period, and many scholars link the debasement with the plague's impact on mining and taxation. Absolute numbers depend on the analytical method: Walker's figures are higher than modern bulk analyses.
scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994)

coinage.standard: denarius at roughly 50% silver from c. 194-196
coinage.text: To pay for the civil wars against Niger and Albinus and for his army pay rise (from 300 to about 450-500 denarii a year), Severus cut the denarius to around half silver: the largest single debasement since its creation. Dio and Herodian record his maxim to his sons, 'enrich the soldiers'. Severan denarii are plentiful, with a wide range of portraits of the family (Julia Domna, Caracalla and Geta as boys) and eastern mint styles. The low-grade silver means that Severan denarii often show copper patches or a grey surface. The debasement made old good-silver denarii worth hoarding: the Shapwick and Réka Devnia hoards show how Gresham's law operated.
scholarship: Walker (1978)
Butcher and Ponting (2014)

coinage.standard: antoninianus c. 5.1 g (one and a half denarii in weight) at about 50% silver, probably tariffed at two denarii; aureus cut to 1/50 lb (c. 6.5 g)
coinage.text: In 215 Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, distinguished by the emperor's radiate crown (and, for empresses, a crescent under the bust), the double-value marks also used on the dupondius. Its ancient name is unknown: 'antoninianus' is a modern coinage from a phrase in the Historia Augusta. Since it weighed only 1.5 denarii but was worth 2, it was a disguised debasement to fund his pay rise and wars. Elagabalus abandoned it c. 219; Pupienus and Balbinus revived it in 238 and under Gordian III it replaced the denarius as the main silver coin, the denarius ceasing as a regular coin by c. 241. The radiate crown is thus the key to recognising the double denomination in the 3rd century, including radiate dupondii and double sestertii.
scholarship: Abdy and others, RIC IV / revisions
Bland, 'Coinage and currency in the 3rd century', in The Roman Imperial Coinage: an Introduction (2012)

coinage.t: The unstable gold of the 3rd century
coinage.text: After Caracalla's aureus at 1/50 lb, gold weights became erratic. Gordian III and Philip struck aurei around 4.5-5 g; under Trebonianus, Valerian and Gallienus weights ran from under 1 g to over 7 g, suggesting gold was valued by weight rather than face. Gallienus also struck radiate binios (double aurei) and spectacular gold multiples. Postumus' gold from the Gallic mints was the best of the period. Aurelian restored an aureus near 1/50 lb; Diocletian set it at 1/60 lb (marked Ξ on some coins), and Constantine's solidus at 1/72 lb ended the instability. Third-century gold is rare and expensive; die studies show that much of it was struck for donatives and largesse to the army.
scholarship: Bland, 'The development of gold and silver coin denominations, AD 193-253', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996
Callu, La politique monétaire des empereurs romains de 238 à 311 (1969)

coinage.t: The double sestertius and the end of the sestertius
coinage.text: Trajan Decius introduced a radiate double sestertius (c. 250), heavier than the sestertius and marked by the radiate crown, perhaps to restore the value of the bronze as the silver collapsed. Postumus revived it in Gaul (260s) with a superb series of large radiate pieces, often struck on old sestertii. Ordinary sestertii shrank and grew rarer through the 250s and ended under Gallienus; Aurelian struck a last small issue. The disappearance of SC bronze in the 260s, along with the city coinages of the East, marks the end of the Augustan currency system and the reduction of the whole system to a single debased radiate coin.
scholarship: Bastien, Le monnayage de bronze de Postume (1967)
Estiot, 'Aurélien et Tacite', in Ripostiglio della Venèra (1995)

coinage.t: The great debasement of the antoninianus
coinage.standard: c. 45-50% silver under Gordian III; c. 40% under Philip; falling to about 15% under Valerian and to 2-5% under Gallienus' sole reign (260-268); 1-2% under Claudius II and Quintillus
coinage.text: As military crises multiplied, the radiate coin was debased step by step. Under Valerian and Gallienus the decline turned into a collapse; by the late 260s antoniniani were bronze coins with a thin silver wash applied by surface enrichment (blanching), which wears off quickly and gives the dark look of most coins of the period. Coins were also struck on smaller, more irregular flans and in vastly greater numbers at more mints (Milan, Siscia, Cyzicus, the Gallic mints). Prices in Egyptian papyri jump after c. 270, suggesting that confidence finally broke. For collectors this period offers huge variety at low cost, with the challenge of finding coins with their silvering intact. Hoards such as Cunetio, Normanby and Frome are the main evidence.
scholarship: Walker (1978)
Rathbone, 'Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996
Bland, 'The coinage of Gallienus', 2012

coinage.t: The end of the civic and provincial coinages
coinage.text: Hundreds of Greek cities had struck their own bronze under Rome. Production peaked under the Severans and in the 240s, then fell away in the 250s and 260s: the last widespread civic issues date to Gallienus, and the very last, at Perge and Side in Pamphylia, to Tacitus (275-276). Alexandria kept its tetradrachms until Diocletian's reform (296/7). The causes debated include the debasement of the imperial radiate (which made civic bronze uneconomic), the cost of festivals, and changes in the cities' finances. The disappearance of the civic coinages removed a vast store of local imagery (temples, festivals, river gods) and a key source on civic titles.
scholarship: Howgego, Heuchert and Burnett (eds.), Coinage and Identity in the Roman Provinces (2005)
Roman Provincial Coinage online (Oxford)

coinage.t: Alexandrian tetradrachms and the closed currency of Egypt
coinage.standard: billon tetradrachm c. 12-13 g, falling to c. 8 g; silver c. 25% under Tiberius to under 1% in the 270s
coinage.text: Egypt kept a currency of its own, exchanged at the border. Tetradrachms resumed under Tiberius in AD 19/20 and were dated by regnal year (L + numeral), which makes them precisely dated documents. Big bronze drachms of Antoninus Pius with zodiac signs, Hercules' labours and Nilotic scenes are a celebrated series. Under Claudius II and Aurelian the tetradrachm became nearly pure bronze. Diocletian's reform ended the system c. 296/7, a change that, with the revolt of Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus in 297-298, may reflect resistance to new taxes. Tetradrachms are common (they turn up in huge hoards) and an excellent, cheap way to collect 3rd-century portraits including obscure emperors.
scholarship: Christiansen, The Roman Coins of Alexandria (1988)
Geissen and Weiser, Katalog alexandrinischer Kaisermünzen (Cologne, 1974-1983)

coinage.text: In Britain and northern Gaul the coins of Tetricus I and II and Claudius II's DIVO CLAVDIO consecration issues were copied on a massive scale in the 270s-280s, producing 'barbarous radiates' from near-official size down to tiny 'minims' a few millimetres across. They fill the gap left by the demonetisation of Gallic coin after Aurelian's reform and before Carausius' coinage. Their crude, often fantastic designs (garbled legends, stick-figure reverses) make them a cult collecting area. Similar waves of imitation followed later: copies of the FEL TEMP REPARATIO falling horseman (350s), and 'minimissimi' in 5th-century Britain and the Mediterranean.
scholarship: Boon, 'Counterfeit coins in Roman Britain', in Casey and Reece (eds.) 1974
Davies, 'Barbarous radiates', BAR 1992

coinage.t: The revolt of the mint workers at Rome
coinage.text: Early in Aurelian's reign the moneyers of Rome, led by the rationalis Felicissimus, rose in revolt. The sources say they had debased the coin (or embezzled silver) and rose when Aurelian moved to punish them; the fighting on the Caelian hill killed thousands of his soldiers (Aurelius Victor gives 7,000). Aurelian crushed them, closed the mint temporarily and later reorganised production: Rome's role as the dominant mint ended and new mints (Ticinum, Serdica, Cyzicus, Tripolis) took a greater share. The revolt helps explain the abrupt drop in quality around 270 and the urgency of Aurelian's reform of 274.
scholarship: Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1 (2004)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

coinage.standard: reformed radiate c. 3.9 g with c. 5% silver; marked XXI (KA in the East); aureus c. 1/50 lb
coinage.text: After reuniting the empire Aurelian issued a reformed radiate of improved weight and a guaranteed silver content of about 5%, marked XXI in Latin mints and KA in Greek ones (and occasionally XX). The meaning of the mark is still debated: 20 parts of copper to 1 of silver (1:20), or 'twenty units' (sesterces or nummi) to one coin, or a tariff of 20 asses. At Rome he also struck a laureate 'denarius' and some sestertii. The reformed coin carried new imperial imagery: Sol Invictus (ORIENS AVG), RESTITVTOR ORBIS, CONCORDIA MILITVM, and the dominus et deus titulature. All mints used officina letters and the XXI mark, creating the first empire-wide system of mint control marks. The reform did not stop inflation: papyri show prices rising after 274.
scholarship: Estiot, Monnaies de l'Empire romain XII.1 (2004)
Göbl, Die Münzprägung des Kaisers Aurelianus (1993)

coinage.standard: aureus c. 5.45 g; argenteus c. 3.4 g of fine silver; nummus c. 10 g with c. 4% silver
coinage.text: Diocletian rebuilt the coinage on uniform lines. A gold aureus at 60 to the pound (some marked Ξ, the Greek numeral 60) and a pure silver argenteus at 96 to the pound (some marked XCVI), in effect a return to Nero's denarius, headed a system whose workhorse was a large silvered bronze coin (c. 10 g, 27-28 mm), conventionally called the follis (its ancient name was probably nummus). A smaller radiate (no silver, without the XXI) and a laureate fraction completed it. The same reverse types were struck everywhere, above all GENIO POPVLI ROMANI (the Genius of the Roman people), and portraits became blocky and uniform, so that the four Tetrarchs are sometimes identifiable only by legend. Every coin carried a mint mark and officina letter. Alexandria's separate coinage ended. The 294 date rests on hoard evidence and the overall reform of mints; some components may have started earlier (the argenteus perhaps 293).
scholarship: Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)
Abdy, 'The Tetrarchy', in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)

coinage.text: An inscription from Aphrodisias preserves an imperial edict, effective 1 September 301, that changed the face values of coins: on the usual reconstruction the argenteus was raised to 100 denarii communes (a unit of account) and the nummus to 25, roughly doubling their value. It warns that debts contracted before the change were to be paid at the old rates. A private letter on papyrus (P. Ryl. IV 607) shows someone rushing to spend 'Italian money' before it lost half its value, evidence that the change could also be a reduction for some coins. The currency edict prepared the ground for the Price Edict issued three months later.
scholarship: Erim, Reynolds and Crawford, 'Diocletian's currency reform: a new inscription', JRS 61 (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

coinage.text: Issued in November-December 301 in the names of all four Tetrarchs, the Edictum de pretiis rerum venalium fixed maximum prices for over a thousand goods and services in denarii communes: a modius of wheat at 100, a pound of pork at 12, a day's wage for a farm labourer at 25 plus food, a pound of gold at 72,000, a pound of purple silk at 150,000, sea freight rates by route. Its preamble denounces profiteers who raised prices where the army passed. Lactantius, hostile, says much blood was shed over trifles, goods vanished from the market and the law had to be abandoned. Fragments survive almost entirely from the Greek East (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Aezani and more than 40 other sites). For historians it is the richest single source on the late Roman price structure; for numismatists it fixes the relationship of gold to the unit of account.
scholarship: Lauffer, Diokletians Preisedikt (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

coinage.text: In the civil wars after Diocletian's abdication the nummus was repeatedly reduced, each ruler on his own timetable, so that coins of the same nominal value vary greatly in size between mints and years. Constantine's western reductions of 307 and 310 came first; Maxentius kept heavier coins for a time; Licinius' eastern IOVI CONSERVATORI coins (313-324) are small. Reverse types proliferate: SOLI INVICTO COMITI (Constantine's patron Sol, to c. 318-320), GENIO POP ROM, IOVI CONSERVATORI, MARTI CONSERVATORI, VIRTVS EXERCIT (with VOT XX standard, 318-320), BEATA TRANQVILLITAS (altar, 321-324). Weight, diameter and type allow fine dating, and these coins are cheap enough to assemble long chronological runs.
scholarship: Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
King, 'The fourth century coinage', in King and Wigg (eds.) 1996

coinage.standard: 1/72 Roman pound (c. 4.5 g) of nearly pure gold
coinage.text: Around 309-310 Constantine, then ruling Gaul and Britain from Trier, began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the pound in place of Diocletian's 60. Its introduction in the West is dated by Trier issues; it spread to the East after the defeat of Licinius (324), when Constantine seized the eastern treasuries and confiscated temple treasures. The solidus became the most stable coin in history: it kept its standard for 700 years, was accepted from Britain to China, and gave its name to the soldier (soldato, soldier) and the 'sou'. Taxes were increasingly assessed and paid in gold (adaeratio), which pulled gold into fiscal circulation. Contemporary critics (the anonymous De Rebus Bellicis) blamed Constantine's gold for widening the gulf between rich and poor.
scholarship: Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001)
Depeyrot, Les monnaies d'or de Dioclétien à Constantin I (1995)

coinage.t: Late Roman silver: siliqua and miliarensis
denominations: siliqua (c. 3.4 g, reduced to c. 2 g)
coinage.text: Constantine reintroduced regular silver alongside the solidus. The coin conventionally called the siliqua (about 3.4 g, later reduced to about 2 g under Constantius II, c. 355) and the heavy and light miliarenses were mainly donative coins, struck for distributions to the army at accessions and anniversaries, which explains their vota legends (VOTIS V MVLTIS X). The names are modern matches with terms in the sources (siliqua as 1/24 of a solidus, miliarense as 1/1000 of a pound of gold) and the matches are uncertain. From the 360s silver carries PS (pusulatum, refined) in the mark. Siliquae were the main silver coin in Britain to its end and were clipped in the 5th century. Western siliquae of the Valentinianic and Theodosian houses with VRBS ROMA (Roma seated) and VIRTVS ROMANORVM are common; the miliarensis is scarce.
scholarship: Kent, RIC VIII (1981)
Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)

coinage.t: VRBS ROMA, CONSTANTINOPOLIS and GLORIA EXERCITVS (330-341)
coinage.text: To mark the dedication of Constantinople (11 May 330) every mint struck two 'city commemoratives' in parallel: VRBS ROMA (helmeted Roma / she-wolf and twins) and CONSTANTINOPOLIS (Constantinopolis helmeted with sceptre / Victory on a prow), in vast numbers until 337 and beyond. Alongside, the standard type was GLORIA EXERCITVS with two soldiers and two standards (330-335), then with one standard (335-341), a reduction marked by a lighter coin. Small symbols in the standard (chi-rho, wreath, letters) distinguish issues. Collectors use these common coins to learn the late Roman mint system, since nearly every mint and officina can be collected.
scholarship: Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
Kent, RIC VIII (1981)

coinage.t: How to read a late Roman mint mark
coinage.text: From 294 almost every coin carries in the exergue a mark built from (1) an optional prefix: SM (sacra moneta, sacred mint), P (pecunia) or M (moneta); (2) the mint abbreviation (TR Trier, LVG Lyon, ARL or CON Arles, R or RM Rome, AQ Aquileia, SIS Siscia, SIRM Sirmium, TS or TES Thessalonica, H or HT Heraclea, CONS Constantinople, N or NIC Nicomedia, K Cyzicus, ANT Antioch, ALE Alexandria, K or PK Carthage, T Ticinum, OST Ostia, LON or PLN London, AMB Amiens, MD Milan, RV Ravenna); (3) an officina mark, Latin in the West (P, S, T, Q) and Greek in the East (A, B, Γ, Δ, Є, S, Z, H, Θ, I, IA); and (4) field symbols or letters marking sub-issues. Precious-metal marks add OB (gold, obryzum, and the Greek numeral 72) or PS (silver, pusulatum). Traps: CON with a Latin letter in front is Arles; CONS with a Greek letter after is Constantinople; SMH is Heraclea, SMN is Nicomedia; COMOB on gold is used by many mints. RIC VI-X tabulate every mark.
scholarship: RIC VI-X
Sear, Roman Coins and their Values IV-V

coinage.text: Emperors took public vows (vota) for their own welfare at fixed intervals, discharged at quinquennalia, decennalia and vicennalia. Coins record them: VOT V (vows for five years taken), VOT X MVLT XX (ten-year vows fulfilled, twenty undertaken), VOT XXX MVLT XXXX. Because the vows were taken at anniversaries, often in advance, the numbers date coins to within a few years: Constantine's VOT XX coins of 315-320, Theodosius II's VOT XX MVLT XXX solidi with a long cross (c. 420-422), the VOT X MVLT XV of Arcadius and Honorius. Caveat: vows could be anticipated by a year or two, and junior emperors' vows ran from their own accession, which can mislead.
scholarship: Kent, RIC VIII introduction (1981)
Chastagnol, 'Les années régnales de Maximien Hercule', RN 1967

coinage.text: The coinage turned Christian slowly. Sol Invictus remained on Constantine's coins until c. 318-320; the chi-rho first appears as a small mark on the helmet of the Ticinum silver medallion of 315 and as a field mark in the 320s, and on the labarum piercing a serpent (SPES PVBLIC, Constantinople, c. 327). Constantine's posthumous coins (337) show him veiled and ascending in a quadriga with the hand of God reaching down: a hybrid of pagan consecration and Christian heaven. Magnentius made the chi-rho the whole reverse (353). Theodosius II's solidi with Victory holding a long jewelled cross (c. 420) put the cross at the centre; Tiberius II replaced Victory with the cross on steps (578); Justinian II's Christ portrait (692) falls after 641. The pace of change is a gauge of how cautiously emperors moved in public religion.
scholarship: Bruun, 'The Christian signs on the coins of Constantine', Arctos 1962
Grierson, Byzantine Coins (1982)

coinage.t: FEL TEMP REPARATIO (348) and the bronze reforms of the 350s
coinage.standard: large coin c. 5.3 g with a small silver content; reduced in 352/3 and again c. 355
coinage.text: For the 1,100th anniversary of Rome (348) Constans and Constantius II issued new bronze with the slogan FEL TEMP REPARATIO ('the restoration of happy times'), each denomination with its own type: the emperor dragging a barbarian from a hut, a phoenix on a globe or pyre, the emperor on a galley steered by Victory, and above all a soldier spearing a fallen horseman. Names such as maiorina and centenionalis come from laws in the Theodosian Code (title 9.23, on transport of money), and matching them to coins is uncertain. The falling horseman type became the standard eastern coin of the 350s, shrinking steadily, and it was copied massively in Britain and Gaul. Gallus Caesar's portraits and Julian's early Caesar coins belong to this series.
scholarship: Kent, RIC VIII (1981)
Carson, 'The reform of the bronze coinage under Constans and Constantius II'

coinage.t: The Valentinianic reform of gold and silver (c. 366-368)
coinage.text: After Procopius' revolt (365-366), during which coins of doubtful purity were struck, Valentinian I and Valens tightened control of precious metals. Gold received in taxes was to be melted into bullion before reuse, refined gold was struck at mints that followed the court (the comitatus), and coins carried OB (obryzum, refined gold) and PS (refined silver). COMOB became the standard gold mark (COM for comitatus or the comes sacrarum largitionum, plus OB), and later CONOB for Constantinople. The reform helps explain why later 4th-century gold is so pure and why gold minting shifted with the emperors' movements between Trier, Milan, Sirmium and Antioch.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985) 386-394
Pearce, RIC IX (1951)

coinage.text: Introduced under Theodosius I (from c. 383), the tremissis replaced the 1.5-scripulum piece as the small gold denomination and became the dominant gold coin of the Germanic successor kingdoms of the West, where Merovingian, Visigothic and Lombard rulers copied it for centuries. Typical late Roman reverse: Victory advancing with wreath and globus cruciger, VICTORIA AVGVSTORVM; Byzantine tremisses show a cross. The 37 Merovingian tremisses of Sutton Hoo show the coin's long afterlife.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)

coinage.t: The late Roman AE4 and the collapse of the bronze
coinage.standard: AE4 c. 1-1.5 g, 11-13 mm, falling below 1 g in the 5th century
coinage.text: From the 380s the main bronze became a tiny coin, SALVS REIPVBLICAE (Victory dragging a captive) and VICTORIA AVGGG, and after 395 the larger AE2 was abolished. The West stopped sending fresh bronze to Britain after c. 402, which is why Romano-British site finds end abruptly. In the 5th century, minimi of Leo I, Zeno and the Vandals, with monograms or a cross in a wreath, sank below a gram; one solidus was worth some 7,000 nummi by the end of the century. The reform of Anastasius (498) finally created multiple-nummus coins to make the small change usable again.
scholarship: Kent, RIC X (1994)
Reece, The Coinage of Roman Britain (2002)

coinage.t: Clipped siliquae in late Roman Britain
coinage.text: Most siliquae found in Britain from the late 4th and early 5th centuries have had their edges clipped, sometimes so severely that the legend vanishes and the portrait is cut. Clipping went on after the flow of new coin stopped (c. 402-410) and seems to have been tolerated, perhaps systematic: it produced silver for imitations or for bullion while keeping the clipped coins in circulation. The Hoxne hoard, with over 14,000 siliquae nearly all clipped, is the main evidence, and the degree of clipping helps date hoards. Clipping was almost unknown on the Continent, which marks Britain's isolation in the last Roman decades.
scholarship: Guest, The Late Roman Gold and Silver Coins from the Hoxne Treasure (2005)
Abdy, 'After Patching', in Hunter and Painter (eds.) 2013

coinage.text: Large bronze medallions with a raised rim and a deep groove (contorno) around the edge, made in Rome in the later 4th and 5th centuries, perhaps as New Year's gifts or tokens connected with the circus games. They show emperors of the distant past (Nero, Trajan), Alexander the Great, Homer, Apuleius and charioteers, with pagan myths, circus scenes and the palm monogram (PE). Often linked with the pagan senatorial aristocracy of Rome (the circle of Symmachus), though the connection is debated. They are not coins. Rare, and copied in modern times.
scholarship: Alföldi and Alföldi, Die Kontorniat-Medaillons (1976-1990)
Mittag, Alte Köpfe in neuen Händen (1999)

coinage.text: Medallions were special issues outside the circulating system, struck from the 2nd century (Hadrian and the Antonines produced large bronze medallions, sometimes bimetallic with an orichalcum centre and copper ring) to the Byzantine period. Late Roman gold multiples (from 1.5 to 9 solidi and larger) were imperial gifts to officers and allied kings: the Beaurains (Arras) medallion of Constantius I, the Szilágysomlyó medallions of Valens, the 36-solidus medallion of Justinian (stolen from the Cabinet des Médailles in 1831 and melted; electrotypes survive). They carry ambitious iconography (imperial adventus, largitio scenes, triumphs) and are documents of court art and diplomacy.
scholarship: Gnecchi, I medaglioni romani (1912)
Toynbee, Roman Medallions (1944)

coinage.text: Imperial women appear on coins in a sequence that tracks their public status. Livia appears anonymously (as Pax or Salus) and then named under Tiberius and as DIVA AVGVSTA under Claudius; Agrippina the Younger shares the obverse with Nero in 54; the Flavian and Trajanic women (Domitia, Plotina, Marciana) begin regular series. The Faustinas, Lucilla, Crispina, Julia Domna (with MATER CASTRORVM), Julia Maesa, Julia Mamaea, Otacilia Severa, Salonina and Severina carry dynastic and religious messages. In the 4th century Helena and Fausta (324-326) and later Flaccilla, Eudoxia, Pulcheria, Galla Placidia, Licinia Eudoxia, Ariadne and Sophia appear, often with the hand of God crowning them. The empress's crescent under the bust marks a double denomination in the 3rd century. Coins of empresses are a principal source for women's honorific titles (Augusta, Mater castrorum, Diva).
scholarship: Kleiner, 'Women and family life on Roman imperial coinage'
Brubaker and Tobler, 'The gender of money', Gender and History 12 (2000)

coinage.text: When an emperor or member of his family was deified, the mint issued commemoratives with DIVO or DIVVS and the symbols of apotheosis: an eagle (for an emperor) or peacock (for an empress) carrying the soul aloft, a multi-storey funeral pyre (rogus), an altar, a carpentum (ceremonial carriage) drawn by mules or elephants, the deified figure on a flying eagle. Decius' series of c. 250-251 restoring coins of eleven deified emperors (DIVO AVGVSTO to DIVO ALEXANDRO) and Claudius II's DIVO CLAVDIO coins (the most copied coins in Britain) are celebrated groups. The last pagan-style consecration issue is Constantine's (337), already infused with Christian imagery. Consecration coins are a primary source for the imperial cult.
scholarship: Gesche, 'Die Divinisierung der römischen Kaiser in ihrer Funktion als Herrschaftslegitimation'
Price, 'From noble funerals to divine cult', in Cannadine and Price (eds.) Rituals of Royalty (1987)

coinage.text: The successor kingdoms kept the Roman system. The Vandals at Carthage left gold to the emperor but struck silver and bronze with royal names and value marks (N XLII, N XXI, N XII). In Italy Odoacer and the Ostrogoths struck gold in the name of the eastern emperor, adding their own monograms on silver and bronze, and revived large bronze at Rome: 40-nummi pieces with INVICTA ROMA and the she-wolf, or an eagle, deliberately evoking the old sestertius. Theodahad's bronze with his own moustached portrait wearing a closed crown and Baduila (Totila)'s coins with his bust are rare exceptions to the convention of not portraying the king. These coinages are vital evidence for the political relationship with Constantinople.
scholarship: Grierson and Blackburn, Medieval European Coinage I (1986)
Metlich, The Coinage of Ostrogothic Italy (2004)

coinage.standard: first series follis c. 8-9 g (498); doubled to c. 17-18 g in c. 512
coinage.text: Marcellinus Comes records under 498 that Anastasius issued coins 'which the Romans call terunciani and the Greeks follares' and so made an exchange that pleased the people. He replaced the worthless nummus with multiples marked by large Greek numerals: M (40), K (20), I (10) and later Є (5), with the mint and officina below. After a first light series, the coins were doubled in weight around 512. The reform, partly anticipated by the Vandal and Ostrogothic coins of value, created the standard Byzantine bronze system and, by fixing the follis to the solidus, eased small transactions in the cities. Collectors date Anastasian folles to the light or heavy series by size and officina marks. It was part of a broader fiscal programme: the same year Anastasius abolished the hated chrysargyron.
scholarship: Grierson, DOC I (1966)
Metcalf, The Origins of the Anastasian Currency Reform (1969)

coinage.t: Justinian's dated folles and facing busts (538/9)
coinage.standard: follis increased to c. 22-25 g (538/9), reduced from c. 542
coinage.text: In Justinian's 12th regnal year (538/9) the follis became heavier and changed design: a facing bust of the emperor in helmet and cuirass holding a cross on globe, and on the reverse the value letter M with ANNO and the regnal year (XII, XIII...). Byzantine bronze is therefore dated by year from 538 to the 7th century. These massive folles, the largest Roman bronze since the 3rd-century sestertius, were reduced in weight from c. 542, probably owing to the fiscal shock of the Justinianic plague, and the reduction itself is visible year by year. The solidus also changed to a facing bust in the 530s-540s. Dated folles let collectors follow mint output year by year, a rare quantitative window on the 6th-century state.
scholarship: Grierson, DOC I (1966)
Hahn, Moneta Imperii Byzantini I-III (1973-1981)

coinage.text: From Justinian to the 7th century the Constantinople mint struck small numbers of solidi below the standard of 24 siliquae, marked in the exergue OB XX (20 siliquae), OB*+ (22) or with other signs (23). They are found mostly outside the empire, in Gaul, the Rhineland and Scandinavia, and their purpose is debated: trade with Frankish markets where gold was valued differently, diplomatic payments, or wages. Collectors should not confuse them with clipped coins or with Merovingian imitations.
scholarship: Adelson, Light Weight Solidi and Byzantine Trade in the Sixth and Seventh Centuries (1957)

coinage.text: Tiberius II replaced the Victory, or the angel holding a cross that had stood on the solidus since Justin I, with a cross potent set on four steps, often taken to represent the cross erected on Golgotha. It became the standard Byzantine gold reverse for over a century. Tiberius also restored more classical portraits and was later remembered for his generosity: chroniclers say he distributed vast sums and found treasure in the palace. The cross on steps lets a collector tell his solidi from those of Justin II at a glance.
scholarship: Grierson, DOC I (1966)

coinage.text: In 615, with the Persians at Chalcedon, Heraclius introduced a large silver coin of 6 grammata (hence hexagram), with the legend DEVS ADIVTA ROMANIS ('God help the Romans') around a cross on a globe set on steps, and on the obverse the emperor with his son Heraclius Constantine. The Chronicon Paschale records that it was introduced in that year and that imperial salaries were thereafter paid at half their former rate in the new coin. In 622 Heraclius melted church plate to coin (Theophanes AM 6113), feeding the hexagram's production. It was struck in large numbers through the Persian war and into the reign of Constans II, then declined; it is the main Byzantine silver coin of the 7th century and a direct witness to the crisis that nearly destroyed the empire.
scholarship: Grierson, DOC II (1968)
Yannopoulos, L'hexagramme (1978)

coinage.text: The war with Persia (602-628) and the loss of Syria and Egypt reduced the follis to a light, carelessly struck coin, very often overstruck on earlier folles (especially Phocas', whose memory Heraclius condemned) without removing the old design. Antioch closed in 610, Alexandria passed to the Persians (618/19-629), Thessalonica, Nicomedia and Cyzicus closed by c. 630, leaving Constantinople, Carthage, Ravenna, Sicily and Alexandria (after 629) as the working mints. Emergency mints at Seleucia and Isaura (615-618) show the front line. A typical Heraclian follis shows three standing figures (Heraclius, Heraclius Constantine, Heraclonas) with M and ANNO on the reverse; regnal dates continue but are frequently illegible.
scholarship: Grierson, DOC II (1968)
Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

coinage.t: Forgeries and how collectors detect them
coinage.text: Ancient coins have been faked since the Renaissance: Paduan 'Paduans' by Giovanni Cavino (16th c.) imitated sestertii and are now collected themselves; Carl Wilhelm Becker (1772-1830) cut hundreds of dies of rarities; 20th-century 'Slavey' and other Bulgarian workshops, Lebanese and Chinese factories produce struck and cast fakes of high quality today. Cast copies show soft details, pitting, a seam on the edge and low weight; transfer-die and struck fakes can be detected by die studies, by comparing with published die pairs (Crawford, RIC and specialist corpora), by fabric and flan shape, and increasingly by metallurgical analysis. Tooling (re-engraving a worn coin) and smoothing are more insidious frauds. Classic fake targets: EID MAR, Social War denarii, Caesar portraits, Judaea Capta sestertii, Otho sestertii (none genuine exist), Pertinax and Didius Julianus aurei, Uranius Antoninus, the Tetrici gold, Magnus Maximus solidi. Provenance and good references are the best defences.
scholarship: Hill, Becker the Counterfeiter (1924-1925)
Klawans, An Introduction to Ancient and Medieval Counterfeit Coins (1977)
IBSCC / Forgery Network
